## SI Holomorphic Boundary conditions and LLL-like wavefunctions

In this section we prove a number of results involving ideal band geometry that we claimed in the main text. First we prove the generality of the boundary conditions (10) for a single band with $C>0$ . Then we use a similar argument to Ref. [29], which assumed a gauge-equivalent version of (10), to show that all single $C=1$ bands have an LLL form, in the sense of (11).

### SI.1 Classification of holomorphic boundary conditions

We begin by showing that for a single ideal band with Chern number $C>0$ it is always possible to perform a gauge transformation $u_{k}\to\lambda_{k}u_{k}$ such that

$$ \Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)=\lambda_{k+G}\lambda^{-1}_{k}\Xi^{\text{(LG)}}_{\bm{G}}(k-k_{0}) $$

where ${\bm{k}}_{0}\simeq{\bm{k}}_{0}+{\bm{G}}_{i}/C$ is a vector in the $C^{2}$ -fold reduced first BZ and

$$ \Xi^{\text{(LG)}}_{{\bm{G}}_{1}}(k)=\exp(2\pi i C k/G_2),\qquad\Xi^{\text{(LG)}}_{{\bm{G}}_{2}}(k)=1. $$

We have added a superscript (LG), relative to the main text, to distinguish the choice (S2) from other boundary conditions written in this section.

To our knowledge, (S1) requires the use of some type of cohomology-based classification; we do not know of an explicit construction. While the Chern number expression

$$ 2\pi C=f_{G_{1}}(k+G_{2})-f_{G_{1}}(k)+f_{G_{2}}(k)-f_{G_{2}}(k+G_{1}),\qquad\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)=e^{if_{\bm{G}}(k)} $$

suggests a linear form of $f(k)$ , such that $C$ is manifestly $k$ -independent as in (S2), we cannot immediately assume such a linear form of $f_{\bm{G}}(k)$ . Indeed, there are nonlinear functions $f_{\bm{G}}(k)$ that yield a $k$ -independent $C$ in (S3). Consider, for example, applying a nonlinear gauge transformation such as $u_{k}\to\exp(ik^3/G_1^3)u_{k}$ : such a transformation preserves $C$ but takes a linear $f_{\bm{G}}(k)$ to a nonlinear $f_{\bm{G}}(k)+3iGk^{2}/G_{1}^{3}$ . It is not clear how to directly show that all non-linearities may be gauged away.

Instead, we rely on the relationship of $\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)$ , often dubbed a “factor of automorphy” in the mathematics literature, to holomorphic line bundles [115, 116]. In particular, we consider the set of $\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)$ that satisfies the cocycle condition

$$ \Xi_{{\bm{G}}+{\bm{G}}^{\prime}}(k)=\Xi_{{\bm{G}}^{\prime}}(k+G)\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k) $$

and consider two choices of $\Xi$ equivalent if they are related by a gauge transformation (S1). Then a choice of $\Xi$ corresponds exactly to a holomorphic line bundle over the Brillouin Zone torus; the gauge redundancy (S1) corresponds exactly to the equivalence of line bundles with different choices of transition functions [115, 116]. The product $\Xi_{1}\Xi_{2}$ corresponds to the tensor product of the associated line bundles, and $\Xi\to\Xi^{-1}$ is the mapping to the dual bundle where all transition functions are inverted. The collection of $\Xi$ up to gauge transformations and the set of holomorphic line bundles form isomorphic Abelian groups.

Holomorphic line bundles on the torus, and therefore boundary conditions $\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)$ up to gauge transformations, can be classified via the Appell-Humbert theorem [115, 116]. The Appell-Humbert theorem yields a single canonical choice of $\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)$ for each distinct line bundle. This canonical choice is usually written in a “symmetric gauge” form rather than our choice (S2), though they may be related through a suitable gauge transformation.

Instead we will use the Appell-Humbert theorem for $C=0$ , which in practice is how the whole theorem is proved [115, 116]. The theorem states that $\Xi^{(0)}$ has $C=0$ in (S3) if and only if it is gauge equivalent to $e^{-i{\bm{G}}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{0}}$ where ${\bm{r}}_{0}$ is an element of the “dual torus”[116], i.e. the real-space unit cell. Now consider some $\Xi_{\bm{G}}({\bm{r}})$ with Chern number $C$ . Then $\Xi^{(0)}=\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)/\Xi^{\text{(LG)}}_{\bm{G}}(k)$ has $C=0$ in (S3) and therefore is equivalent to $e^{-i{\bm{G}}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{0}}$ for some ${\bm{r}}_{0}$ by Appell-Humbert. Therefore, we may always apply a gauge transformation such that

$$ \Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)=e^{-i{\bm{G}}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{0}}\Xi_{\bm{G}}^{\text{(LG)}}(k). $$

We now show how to convert a choice of ${\bm{r}}_{0}$ in the real-space unit cell to a choice of $k_{0}\equiv k_{0}+{\bm{G}}_{i}/C$ for $C\neq 0$ . We perform the gauge transformation

$$ \Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)\to\lambda_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}}\Xi_{\bm{G}}(k)\lambda_{k}^{-1},\qquad\lambda_{k}=\exp(i\bG_2 \cdot\br_0 k/G_2) $$

which has the effect

$$ \Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}}(k)=e^{-i{\bm{G}}_{1}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{0}}\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}}^{\text{(LG)}}(k)\to\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}}^{\text{(LG)}}(k-k_{0}),\qquad\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{2}}(k)=e^{-i{\bm{G}}_{2}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{0}}\to 1 $$

with

$$ {\bm{k}}_{0}=-\frac{A_{\text{BZ}}}{2\pi C}\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{r}}_{0}. $$

Here $A_{\text{BZ}}=\hat{{\bm{z}}}\cdot{\bm{G}}_{1}\times{\bm{G}}_{2}$ is the area of the Brillouin Zone. To simplify the first equation of (S7) we have written ${\bm{r}}_{0}=r_{1,0}{\bm{a}}_{1}+{\bm{r}}_{2,0}{\bm{a}}_{2}$ and identified $-r_{1,0}{\bm{G}}_{2}+r_{2}{\bm{G}}_{1}=-\frac{A_{\bm{z}}}{2\pi}\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{r}}_{0}$ as a map from the unit cell to the first BZ. The further division by $C$ in (S8) ensures that $k_{0}$ is equivalent to $k_{0}+G_{1,2}/C$ because ${\bm{r}}_{0}$ is equivalent to ${\bm{r}}_{0}+{\bm{a}}_{1,2}$ .

### SI.2 LLL form of $C=1$ ideal band wavefunctions

We now show how to prove (11), copied below for convenience. This argument was previously given in Ref. [29]; we are repeating it here so that our discussion is self-contained.

$$ \psi_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}({\bm{r}})=\psi_{{\bm{k}}-({\bm{k}}_{0}-{\bm{k}}^{\text{LLL}}_{0})}({\bm{r}}){\mathcal{N}}_{\alpha}({\bm{r}}). $$

Here $\psi_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}({\bm{r}})=e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{r}}}u_{k}({\bm{r}})$ is the wavefunction for the ideal $C=1$ band of interest written in the holomorphic gauge corresponding to (S2) for some $k_{0}$ . The index $\alpha$ corresponds to a non-positional orbital degree of freedom, for example layer. Similarly, $\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\text{LLL}}({\bm{r}})=e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{r}}}u_{k}^{\text{LLL}}({\bm{r}})$ is the LLL wavefunction written in holomorphic gauge (S2) which is constructed explicitly in the next section.

Consider the ratio

$$ \frac{\psi_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}({\bm{r}})}{\psi^{\text{LLL}}_{{\bm{k}}-({\bm{k}}_{0}-{\bm{k}}_{0}^{\text{LLL}})}({\bm{r}})}=e^{-i({\bm{k}}_{0}-{\bm{k}}_{0}^{\text{LLL}})\cdot{\bm{r}}}\frac{u_{k\alpha}({\bm{r}})}{u^{\text{LLL}}_{k-(k_{0}-k_{0}^{\text{LLL}})}({\bm{r}})}\equiv{\mathcal{N}}_{\alpha k}({\bm{r}}). $$

Here, the final equality defines ${\mathcal{N}}_{\alpha k}({\bm{r}})$ , as a holomorphic function which we now show is $k$ -independent. Note that ${\mathcal{N}}_{\alpha k}({\bm{r}})$ is a periodic under $k\to k+G_{i}$ because $\psi_{{\bm{k}}}$ and $\psi^{\text{LLL}}_{{\bm{k}}-({\bm{k}}_{0}-{\bm{k}}^{\text{LLL}}_{0})}$ have the same boundary conditions.

Furthermore, ${\mathcal{N}}_{\alpha k}({\bm{r}})$ can have at most one pole: the wavefunction $u^{\text{LLL}}_{{\bm{k}}}({\bm{r}})$ , for fixed ${\bm{r}}$ , only has a single zero in the Brillouin Zone. The lack of extra zeros may be seen by through the explicit construction in the next section or proved on general grounds through the expression [29, 31]

$$ 2\pi iC=\oint_{\partial\text{BZ}}\ln u_{k}({\bm{r}})dk=2\pi iN_{z}. $$

where the integral around the boundary of the Brillouin Zone counts the number of zeros $N_{z}$ of $u_{k}({\bm{r}})$ in the first BZ. The relation to the Chern number is recovered by computing the integral using the boundary conditions of $u$ and recovering (S3) [29, 31].

Periodic holomorphic functions with only one pole per unit cell are constant. To see this, note that Cauchy’s integral theorem $\oint_{\text{BZ}}N_{k\alpha}({\bm{r}})dk$ computes the residue of the pole but this integral vanishes since $N_{k}$ is periodic. Thus $N_{k}$ is bounded, but bounded holomorphic functions are constant by Liouville’s theorem. We have therefore shown that $N_{k\alpha}({\bm{r}})$ is $k$ -independent, such that we recover (S9).

We emphasize that this argument relies on $C=1$ ; higher Chern bands are not related to each other by $k$ -independent factors because their ratio may be an elliptic function with more than one pole per unit cell (with total residue zero). This complexity is difficult to work with, which is one way to view the motivation to decompose higher Chern bands into multiple $C=1$ bands.

## SII Magnetic Bloch states of the Lowest Landau level

In this section we review the form of magnetic translations and magnetic Bloch states in symmetric electromagnetic gauge. We then construct the LLL wavefunctions with a suitable momentum-space gauge (10) and construct the gauge-dependent magnetic translation form (16).

We take our magnetic field to be a constant value of $B>0$ and choose lattice vectors ${\bm{R}}_{1,2}$ that enclose $2\pi$ flux and corresponding reciprocal lattice vectors ${\bm{Q}}_{1,2}$ such that ${\bm{Q}}_{i}\cdot{\bm{R}}_{j}=2\pi\delta_{ij}$ :

$$ B\hat{{\bm{z}}}\cdot{\bm{R}}_{1}\times{\bm{R}}_{2}=2\pi=B^{-1}\hat{{\bm{z}}}\cdot{\bm{Q}}_{1}\times{\bm{Q}}_{2}. $$

For our applications to higher Chern bands, the lattice vectors ${\bm{R}}$ will describe a $\absolutevalue*{C}$ -fold enlarged real space lattice and the reciprocal lattice vectors ${\bm{Q}}$ will describe the folded Brillouin Zone.

The Hamiltonian is

$$ H=\frac{\absolutevalue*{-i \bnabla- e \bA}^{2}}{2m}=\frac{2}{m}\Pi\overline{\Pi}+\frac{B}{2m},\quad\overline{\Pi}=(-i\overline{\partial}-\overline{A}) $$

where $2\overline{\partial}=\partial_{x}+i\partial_{y}$ and $2\overline{A}=A_{x}+iA_{y}$ . The lowest Landau level is the zero mode space of $\overline{\Pi}$ . The zero mode wavefunctions are of the form

$$ \psi({\bm{r}})=f(z)e^{-K({\bm{r}})} $$

where $-i\overline{\partial}K=\overline{A}$ . We will choose the symmetric gauge vector potential ${\bm{A}}=B(-y,x)$ such that $2\overline{A}=B(-y+ix)=-iBz$ and $K=Bz\overline{z}/4$ .

The magnetic translation operators are given by

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}}=e^{-i\zeta_{{\bm{l}}}({\bm{r}})}e^{{\bm{l}}\cdot{\bm{\nabla}}}, $$

where

$$ {\bm{A}}({\bm{r}}+{\bm{l}})-{\bm{A}}({\bm{r}})={\bm{\nabla}}\zeta_{\bm{l}}({\bm{r}}) $$

From this we can derive the commutation relation

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}_{1}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}_{2}}=e^{iB\hat{z}\cdot{\bm{l}}_{1}\times{\bm{l}}_{2}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}_{2}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}_{1}} $$

such that the magnetic translations commute if ${\bm{l}}_{i}$ are lattice vectors ${\bm{R}}$ due to (S12). Note, however, that there is a subtlety $T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}_{1}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}_{2}}=-T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}_{1}+{\bm{R}}_{2}}$ since the triangle spanned by the points ${\bm{R}}_{1},{\bm{R}}_{2},{\bm{R}}_{1}+{\bm{R}}_{2}$ encloses $\pi$ flux. We therefore take $(T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}_{1}})^{m}(T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}_{2}})^{n}$ to be the Bloch translation associated to the lattice vector $m{\bm{R}}_{1}+n{\bm{R}}_{2}$ , which in general is not the same as $T^{\text{mag}}_{m{\bm{R}}_{1}+n{\bm{R}}_{2}}$ .

Consider Bloch wavefunctions $\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})$ such that

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})=e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}}). $$

On general grounds, using (S17) we have

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}=e^{iB\hat{{\bm{z}}}\cdot{\bm{R}}\times{\bm{l}}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}=e^{iB\hat{{\bm{z}}}\cdot{\bm{R}}\times{\bm{l}}}e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}=e^{i({\bm{k}}-B\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{l}})\cdot{\bm{R}}}e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}}\psi_{\bm{k}} $$

such that $T^{\text{mag}}_{\bm{l}}\psi_{\bm{k}}$ and $\psi_{{\bm{k}}-B\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{l}}}$ have the same eigenvalue under translations. We therefore conclude that $T^{\text{mag}}_{\bm{l}}$ acts as a momentum translation

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{\bm{l}}\psi_{{\bm{k}}}\propto\psi_{{\bm{k}}-B\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{l}}}, $$

where the proportionality constant is gauge dependent because the relative prefactor between $\psi_{\bm{k}}$ and $\psi_{{\bm{k}}-B\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{l}}}$ is gauge dependent. We now move onto gauge-specific calculations, in both the electromagnetic and momentum-space sense.

In our symmetric gauge, we have the translation operators

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{l}}}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}B{\bm{l}}\times{\bm{r}}}e^{{\bm{l}}\cdot{\bm{\nabla}}},\qquad T^{\text{mag}}_{\bm{R}}=\eta_{\bm{R}}T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{R}}} $$

and the wavefunctions [10, 29]

$$ \psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})=\lambda_{k}e^{\frac{i}{2}\overline{k}^{\prime}z}\sigma(z+iB^{-1}k^{\prime})e^{-B\absolutevalue*{z}^{2}/4} $$

where $k^{\prime}=k-k_{0}^{\text{LLL}}$ with $k_{0}^{\text{LLL}}=-({\bm{Q}}_{1}+{\bm{Q}}_{2})/2$ and $\sigma(z)=\sigma(z|R_{1},R_{2})$ is the (modified [117]) Weierstrass sigma function which satisfies

$$ \sigma(-z)=-\sigma(z),\qquad\sigma(z+R)=\eta_{\bm{R}}e^{\frac{B}{2}\overline{R}\left(z+\frac{R}{2}\right)} $$

where $\eta_{\bm{R}}=1$ if ${\bm{R}}/2$ is a lattice vector and $-1$ otherwise. From (S23) it is straightforward to verify the Bloch boundary conditions of (S22). The relations $\hat{{\bm{z}}}\cdot{\bm{R}}\times{\bm{r}}=-\frac{i}{2}(\overline{R}z-R\overline{z})$ and ${\bm{R}}\cdot{\bm{r}}=\frac{1}{2}(\overline{R}z+R\overline{z})$ for transforming between vector and complex notation are helpful here.

The wavefunction (S22) is in a holomorphic gauge; this can be straightforwardly verified by computing $u_{k}({\bm{r}})=e^{-i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{r}}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})=e^{-\frac{i}{2}\overline{k}z}e^{-\frac{i}{2}z\overline{k}}\psi_{\bm{k}}({\bm{r}})$ such that the non-holomorphic $e^{\frac{i}{2}\overline{k}z}$ factor in $\psi$ is cancelled. The holomorphic factor $\lambda_{k}$ parameterizes the remaining holomorphic gauge freedom; we now fix $\lambda_{k}$ such that the boundary conditions of (S22) match (10), (S2) for $k_{0}=0$ . To do this, we simply engineer $\lambda_{k}$ such that $\Xi_{{\bm{Q}}_{2}}(k)=1$ . We obtain

$$ 1=\lambda_{k+Q_{2}}\lambda_{k}^{-1}e^{i\pi+\frac{1}{2B}\overline{Q}_{2}\left(k^{\prime}+\frac{Q_{2}}{2}\right)}\implies\lambda_{k}=\exp\left(-i\pi\frac{k^{\prime}}{Q_{2}}-\frac{\overline{Q}_{2}k^{\prime 2}}{4BQ_{2}}\right). $$

We now compute, using (S12)

$$ \Xi_{{\bm{Q}}_{1}}(k)=\lambda_{k+Q_{1}}\lambda_{k}^{-1}e^{i\pi+\frac{1}{2B}\overline{Q}_{1}\left(k^{\prime}+\frac{Q_{1}}{2}\right)}=e^{-i\pi\frac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}B^{-1}(\overline{Q_{1}}Q_{2}-Q_{1}\overline{Q_{2}})\left(k^{\prime}+\frac{Q_{1}}{2}\right)/Q_{2}\right)=e^{2\pi ik^{\prime}/Q_{2}} $$

such that we obtain the desired boundary conditions (S2) with $k_{0}=k_{0}^{\text{LLL}}=-(Q_{1}+Q_{2})/2$ .

We now compute $c_{\bm{l}}(k)$ where

$$ T^{\text{mag}}_{\bm{l}}\psi_{\bm{k}}=c_{\bm{l}}({\bm{k}})\psi_{{\bm{k}}-B\hat{{\bm{z}}}\times{\bm{l}}}. $$

Through direct computation we obtain

$$ \displaystyle c_{\bm{l}}({\bm{k}}) \displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\lambda_{k-iBl}}\exp\left[\frac{i}{2}l\left(\overline{k}^{\prime}-\frac{iB\overline{l}}{2}\right)\right] \displaystyle=e^{\pi Bl/Q_{2}}\exp\left[\frac{-i}{2}\frac{\overline{Q}_{2}}{Q_{2}}l\left(k^{\prime}-\frac{iBl}{2}\right)+\frac{i}{2}l\left(\overline{k}^{\prime}+\frac{iB\overline{l}}{2}\right)\right] \displaystyle=e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{l}}}e^{\frac{i}{2}({\bm{Q}}_{1}+{\bm{Q}}_{2})\cdot{\bm{l}}}e^{\pi Bl/Q_{2}}\exp\left[-\frac{i}{2}\left(\frac{\overline{Q}_{2}}{Q_{2}}l+\overline{l}\right)\left(k^{\prime}-\frac{iBl}{2}\right)\right] \displaystyle=e^{i{\bm{k}}_{0}^{\text{LLL}}}c_{{\bm{l}}}^{(0)}({\bm{k}}-{\bm{k}}_{0}^{\text{LLL}}) $$

where

$$ c^{(0)}_{\bm{l}}({\bm{k}})=e^{i{\bm{k}}\cdot{\bm{l}}}e^{\frac{i}{2}({\bm{Q}}_{1}+{\bm{Q}}_{2})\cdot{\bm{l}}}e^{\frac{\pi Bl}{Q_{2}}-\frac{i}{2}\left(\frac{\overline{Q}_{2}}{Q_{2}}l+\overline{l}\right)\left(k-\frac{iBl}{2}\right)} $$

as claimed in the main text (16).

## SIII Computation details of $U_{k}$

In this section we construct and prove the uniqueness of the matrix $U_{k}$ (SIII) that hybridizes the folded ideal $C=2$ band into two ideal $C=1$ bands. We find it easier to compute the wavefunction of the ideal bands after decomposition directly, and then organize the coefficients into the matrix $U_{k}$ .

We take a general holomorphic combination

$$ \phi_{\bm{k}}=\alpha_{0}(k)\psi_{\bm{k}}+\alpha_{1}(k)\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{1}/2} $$

and require that

$$ \phi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{1}/2}=\xi_{1,g}(k)\phi_{\bm{k}},\qquad\phi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{2}}=\phi_{\bm{k}} $$

We will find two distinct solutions $\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1}$ ; these two solution sets will comprise the two rows of $U_{k}$ . Inserting (S29) into (S30), we obtain the following conditions for $\alpha_{0,1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{0}(k+G_{1}/2)=\alpha_{1}(k)\xi_{1,g}(k) \displaystyle\alpha_{1}(k+G_{1}/2)\xi_{2,k_{0}}(k)=\alpha_{0}(k)\xi_{1,g}(k) $$

The first equation gives $\alpha_{1}(k)=\alpha_{0}(k+G_{1}/2)\xi^{-1}_{1,g}(k)$ ; further using the second equation, we have

$$ \alpha_{0}(k+G_{1})\xi^{-1}_{1,g}(k+G_{1}/2)\xi_{2,k_{0}}(k)=\alpha_{0}(k)\xi_{1,g}(k), $$

which means that

$$ \frac{\alpha_{0}(k+G_{1})}{\alpha_{0}(k)}=\exp(2\pi i (2k_0-2g+G_1/2)/G_2)=\exp(\beta). $$

for some $k$ -independent $\beta$ . We also have $\alpha(k+G_{2})=\alpha(k)$ from the second equation in (S30). Defining $\alpha_{0}(k)=e^{\gamma(k)}$ then yields

$$ \gamma(k+G_{1})-\gamma(k)=\beta,\qquad\gamma(k+G_{2})-\gamma(k)=2\pi in. $$

Since $\gamma(k)$ has no poles, a contour integral along boundaries of the Brillouin zone yields, via the residue theorem,

$$ \beta G_{2}-2\pi inG_{1}=0. $$

We multiply the wavefunction by an overall constant such that $\alpha_{0}(k=0)=1$ and $\gamma(0)=0$ . We define $\delta(k)=\gamma(k)-\beta k/G_{1}$ such that $\delta(k)$ vanishes on reciprocal lattice vectors $aG_{1}+bG_{2}$ for $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Since $\delta(k)$ is a periodic holomorphic function it must be constant, such that $\delta(0)=0$ , $\delta(k)=0$ and thus $\gamma(k)=2\pi ink/G_{2}$ .

From (S33), we deduce that for each $g$ that satisfies $\exp(2\pi i (2k_0-2g+G_1/2 + n G_1)/G_2)$ (S30). Taking a logarithm, and encoding the associated $2\pi i$ ambiguity with an integer $m$ , we obtain

$$ g=k_{0}+G_{1}/4-nG_{1}/2-mG_{2}/2. $$

The shift in $G_{1}/2$ may be gauged away because ${\bm{G}}_{1}/2$ is now a reciprocal lattice vector (see SI Sec. SI.1). We can then choose $n=0$ such that $\alpha_{0}=1$ . Since ${\bm{G}}_{2}$ is a reciprocal lattice vector, there are two distinct choices are $m=0,1$ . We then obtain the two possible boundary conditions

$$ \xi_{m}=\xi_{1,k_{0}+G_{1}/4-mG_{2}/2}(k)=(-1)^{m}\xi_{1,k_{0}+G_{1}/4}(k) $$

for which the wavefunctions $\phi_{m{\bm{k}}}$ are

$$ \phi_{m{\bm{k}}}=\psi_{\bm{k}}+(-1)^{m}\xi_{1,k_{0}+G_{1}/4}^{-1}(k)\psi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{1}/2}. $$

We may then read off the matrix $U_{k}$

$$ U_{k}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&\xi_{1,k_{0}+G_{1}/4}^{-1}(k)\\
1&\xi_{1,k_{0}+G_{1}/4-G_{2}/2}^{-1}(k)\end{array}\right). $$

## SIV Chern Bands with $C>2$

For $C>2$ bands, a similar procedure can be performed. However, in general we can attempt to generate $r$ bands, in which $r<C$ . We break translation symmetry in ${\bm{a}}_{1}$ direction by $r$ times:

$$ \phi_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{m}\alpha_{m}(k)\psi_{{\bm{k}}+m{\bm{G}}_{1}/r} $$

and try to “diagonalize” the boundary conditions:

$$ \phi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{1}/r}=\xi_{1,g}(k)\phi_{\bm{k}},\qquad\phi_{{\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{2}}=\phi_{\bm{k}} $$

We find that when $r$ doesn’t divide $C$ the two boundary conditions (S41) are not compatible. When $r$ does divide $C$ we find $r$ solutions to (S41), leading to an $r\times r$ holomorphic matrix $U_{k}$ . The resulting bands (S40) have Chern number $C/r$ . We must solve the following equations similar to (S31):

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{0}(k+G_{1}/r)=\alpha_{1}(k)\xi_{C/r,g}(k) \displaystyle\alpha_{1}(k+G_{1}/r)=\alpha_{2}(k)\xi_{C/r,g}(k) \displaystyle\dots \displaystyle\alpha_{r-1}(k+G_{1}/r)\xi_{C,k_{0}}(k)=\alpha_{0}(k)\xi_{C/r,g}(k) $$

All coefficients are fundamentally related to $\alpha_{0}$ . Using techniques analogous to those in the previous section, we find

$$ U_{ml}=\alpha_{ml}(k)=e^{-2\pi iml/r}\prod_{n<l}\xi^{-1}_{C/r,k_{0}+(r-1)G_{1}/2r}(k+nG_{1}/r) $$

We get $r$ bands $\phi_{m{\bm{k}}}$ , each with Chern number $C/r$ , with boundary conditions

$$ \phi_{m({\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{1}/r)}=\xi_{C/r,k_{0}+(r-1)G_{1}/2r}(k)e^{2\pi im/r}\phi_{m{\bm{k}}},\qquad\phi_{m({\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{2})}=\phi_{m{\bm{k}}} $$

We now specialize to the case $r=C$ in order to derive the $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ action. We find that $\phi_{m({\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{2}/2-m{\bm{G}}_{2}/C)}$ all have the same boundary conditions. We thus define

$$ \tilde{\phi}_{m{\bm{k}}}=\phi_{m({\bm{k}}+{\bm{G}}_{2}/2-m{\bm{G}}_{2}/C)} $$

Similar to $C=2$ , these states also form a non-unitary representation of $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ [118], with the similar identification

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{Z} \displaystyle=(T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{a}}_{2}})^{-1}T_{{\bm{a}}_{2}}, \displaystyle\mathsf{X} \displaystyle=(T^{\text{mag}}_{{\bm{a}}_{1}})^{-1}T_{{\bm{a}}_{1}},\,\,\mathsf{Z}\mathsf{X}=e^{2\pi i/C}\mathsf{X}\mathsf{Z} $$

Next, we want to understand the ground state degeneracy in this system. In order to obtain the degeneracy of the $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ ferromagnet in a finite system, we need to identify the $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ irreducible representation for the ground states. One definite element of the ground state manifold is the state with full-polarization in a certain $C=1$ band: $\ket{0}=\mathcal{A}\ket{\phi_{0\bk_1},\phi_{0\bk_2},\dots}$ in which $\mathcal{A}$ antisymmetrizes particles. Since it is fully symmetrized with respect to the $SU(C)$ index, it is part of the irrep expressed by the following Young diagram:

$$ \underbrace{{\hbox{}\hskip 0.0pt\vbox{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=8.74669pt,width=0.3pt,depth=2.18663pt\hbox to10.93333pt{\hfil}\vrule height=8.74669pt,width=0.3pt,depth=2.18663pt\hbox to10.93333pt{\hfil}\vrule height=8.74669pt,width=0.3pt,depth=2.18663pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt\cdots\cdots\hbox{}\hskip 0.0pt\vbox{\vbox{\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=8.74669pt,width=0.3pt,depth=2.18663pt\hbox to10.93333pt{\hfil}\vrule height=8.74669pt,width=0.3pt,depth=2.18663pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt}}_{N_{e}} $$

whose dimension can be calculated by the Hook’s formula:

$$ \textrm{dim\,[$N_{e}$]${}_{C}$}=\frac{(N_{e}+C-1)!}{N_{e}!(C-1)!} $$

As the state $\ket{0}$ will generate all other state in the same irrep under the action of $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ symmetry, this corresponds to the groundstate degeneracy of the system. For $C=2$ , $\textrm{GSD}=N_{e}+1$ .

As with $C=2$ , because the $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ operators involve momentum translations by ${\bm{G}}_{i}/C$ the full $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ degeneracy only appears in finite size $N_{1}{\bm{a}}_{1}\times N_{2}{\bm{a}}_{2}$ systems when both $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ are divisible by $C$ . If only $N_{1}$ or $N_{2}$ are divisible by $C$ , but not the other, there are only $C$ ground states, each one obtained by completely filling one of the $\phi_{m{\bm{k}}}$ bands.

## SV General Unit Cell Expansion

In this section we examine the possibility of expanding the unit cell by a factor of $r$ , but not necessarily entirely along the ${\bm{a}}_{1}$ or ${\bm{a}}_{2}$ direction. We will construct $r$ bands with Chern number $C/r$ , though for the $\mathrm{SU}(C)$ action one should follow the previous procedure and expand the unit cell by a factor of $C$ in both directions.

We call our original lattice vectors ${\bm{a}}_{1},{\bm{a}}_{2}$ and the new lattice vectors ${\bm{a}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{a}}^{\prime}_{2}$ . The original reciprocal lattice vectors are ${\bm{G}}_{1},{\bm{G}}_{2}$ and the new ones ${\bm{G}}^{\prime}_{1},{\bm{G}}^{\prime}_{2}$ . We write down the coordinates of ${\bm{a}}^{\prime}$ in terms of ${\bm{a}}$ :

$$ {\bm{a}}^{\prime}_{i}=\sum_{j}M_{ij}{\bm{a}}_{j} $$

where $M_{ij}$ are integer. $\det M$ is the ratio between the volume of the two unit cells: that is, $\det M=r$ . We take $M$ to have positive determinant to preserve orientation.

We consider the Smith normal form of the matrix $M$ :

$$ M=PRQ,\quad R=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}r_{1}&0\\
0&r_{2}\end{array}\right) $$

in which $P,Q\in SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ and $r_{1}$ divides $r_{2}$ . Physically speaking, it tells us that any expansion of unit cell can be decomposed into three steps: redefining the unit cell in the original lattice, expanding the new cell by $r_{1}\times r_{2}$ times and redefining the unit cell again. Lattice redefinitions do not affect the Chern number or holomorphicity of bands $\phi_{mk}$ , so without loss of generality we may set $P=Q=1$ by choosing an appropriate basis for the original and final unit cell.

Note that $\det R=r=r_{1}r_{2}$ . We will prove that in general such an unit cell expansion for an ideal Chern number $C$ band will generate $r$ ideal bands, each with Chern number $C/r$ .

We have ${\bm{G}}^{\prime}_{1}={\bm{G}}_{1}/r_{1}$ , ${\bm{G}}^{\prime}_{2}={\bm{G}}_{2}/r_{2}$ . We define the wavefunctions in the folded Brillouin zone as

$$ \psi_{lm\mathbf{k}}=\psi_{l{\bm{G}}_{1}^{\prime}+m{\bm{G}}_{2}^{\prime}+{\bm{k}}}, $$

which have the boundary conditions

$$ \displaystyle\left(\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}^{\prime}}({\bm{k}})\right)_{lm,l^{\prime}m^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\delta_{mm^{\prime}}\delta_{l,l^{\prime}+1}\text{ if }1\leq l^{\prime}\leq r_{1}, \displaystyle\left(\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}^{\prime}}({\bm{k}})\right)_{r_{1}m,0m^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\delta_{mm^{\prime}}\xi_{C,k_{0}}({\bm{k}}+m{\bm{G}}_{2}^{\prime}) $$

and

$$ \left(\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{2}^{\prime}}({\bm{k}})\right)_{lm,l^{\prime}m^{\prime}}=\delta_{ll^{\prime}}\delta_{m,m^{\prime}+1\text{mod }n_{2}}. $$

The “eigenfunctions” after we diagonalize both $\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}^{\prime}}$ and $\Xi_{{\bm{G}}_{2}^{\prime}}$ are

$$ \varphi_{\alpha\beta{\bm{k}}}=\sum_{lm}\exp\left(-2\pi i\left(\frac{\alpha l}{r_{1}}+\frac{\beta m}{r_{2}}\right)\right)\prod_{n<l}\xi^{-1}_{C/r_{1},k_{0}+(r_{1}-1)G_{1}/2r_{1}}(k+nG_{1}^{\prime})\psi_{lm{\bm{k}}} $$

for $\alpha\equiv\alpha+r_{1}$ and $\beta\equiv\beta+r_{2}$ . We therefore obtain $r_{1}r_{2}=r$ distinct bands in total as expected. The boundary conditions for $\varphi_{\alpha\beta{\bm{k}}}$ are

$$ \xi_{{\bm{G}}_{1}\alpha\beta}(k)=\exp(2\pi i\frac{\alpha}{r_1})\xi_{C/r_{1},k_{0}+(r_{1}-1)G_{1}/2r_{1}}(k), $$

and

$$ \xi_{{\bm{G}}_{2}\alpha\beta}(k)=\exp(2\pi i\frac{\beta}{r_2}) $$

to convert into the canonical form, we define

$$ \phi_{\alpha\beta{\bm{k}}}=\varphi_{\alpha\beta{\bm{k}}}\exp(-2\pi i\beta k/G_2) $$

These $\phi$ states are holomorphic because they are holomorphic combinations of ideal bands. Furthermore, they have Chern number $C/r$ as may be identified from the boundary condition (S55) and computed through (9).
